newsitem.title: USA: Grant's Municipal Bond Observer - April 18, 1997.
newsitem.headline: Grant's Municipal Bond Observer - April 18, 1997.

text.p: We are not in the business of forecasting interest rates, and here note only that the Federal Reserve has tightened interest rates once, and that our smarties think it will do so again, and even again after that. In the morning mail, we see the Sage Advisory Services' quarterly economic outlook. Reading down the first column, we find, "Only once in recent history has the Fed refrained from implementing more than a single rate increase to cool off the economy."

Again: We do not forecast interest rates, but we do observe, day by day, signs that retail is again interested in municipals, and maybe now flush with their stock market winnings more so than ever. Big dealers say it. Small dealers say it. Retail is back.

Even our own circulation says it. We spoke with an asset manager and new subscriber last week who wanted to know where he could find the bonds we write about. We asked him, "Well, did you see this morning's Blue List?" He, in turn, asked us: "What's the Blue List?"
Municipals, like Ovaltine, are not just for breakfast, or institutions, anymore.

This having being said, the news that interest rates are headed at least temporarily higher is not all bad. In fact, as our Ken Shirley has pointed out to us, bond buyers cannot escape the death grip of mathematics. That is, if a bond buyer buys a bond intending to hold it until maturity and reinvest all the interest payments, then it is a mathematical fact that the buyer will be better off if rates head higher.

To the trader, this is anathema. If he holds an 8% bond and rates go to 12% or more, who wants his 8% bond? True enough. But the trader's horizon is a heartbeat. We well recall the chapter on bond traders in "The Municipal Bond Handbook (1983)", which said, "No trader should ever take a long-term view about a bond. He has to be able to appreciate only a certain moment in time and utilize it to its fullest."

These traders, by the by, were also the same fellows who serendipitously termed the Blue List "a municipal bond novel." Their point was well taken. Traders trade. Investors invest. They do not speculate on the direction of interest rates. We presume here that most buyers are in for the long pull. If our investor buys a 10-year bond with an 8% coupon and rates go up to 12%, and our investor hangs on and reinvests the proceeds, he is always reinvesting at the higher rate. His total return will be 9.17%.

We pause to point out that an investor in a mutual fund, given the prospect of higher rates, might well blanch. The fund, in effect, never matures. If rates are higher at the time the buyer redeems his shares, he faces a loss of principal.

As full-time journalists, and part-time debaters, we are accustomed to people using facts and figures to prove a point, any point. As Ron Ryan of Ryan Labs emphasizes: "People are being mesmerized by formulas and yields. This business is very complex mathematically. Until you can translate all the gibberish into money into total returns it is hard to understand good from bad."

To conclude: Tax-exempt municipal bonds are good. Reinvestment as rates rise is good. And having a clear investment objective is even better. Joe Mysak, Editor of Grant's Municipal Bond Observer (The opinions expressed here are soley that of the author.) (Reprinted with permission from the Interest Rate Publishing Corporation. Grant's Municipal Bond Observer, Vol.4, No.8, April 18, 1997.)
